subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 11 periods = 495 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 8h 15min

periods.activity_title: First Encounter with the Hymn: Reading Aloud

time_bands.activity: Invite students to share what they know about harvest festivals in India — brief open-floor exchange to activate prior experience. Allow two or three voices before moving to the text.

Teacher reads the full poem aloud from the textbook (pp. 173–175) with deliberate pacing, pausing at each stanza change to let students register the shift in speaker. Students follow along silently, tracking the voices — Men, Women, All — as the teacher names them at each stanza.

Teacher asks students to identify which deity is addressed in each stanza and writes their responses on the board: Surya, Varuna, Prithvi, Brahma. Brief whole-class check — no extended discussion yet.

periods.teacher_notes: This is students' first formal encounter with Naidu's hymn; the four-voice structure (Men, Women, All) and the sequential address to Surya, Varuna, Prithvi, and Brahma are the key orientation points. The most common early difficulty is distinguishing the three elemental deities from the universal creator Brahma — keep the board list visible throughout. No prior reading or homework is assumed for this encounter.

periods.activity_title: Main Ideas by Stanza — Comprehension Discussion

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.176): match stanza numbers to their main ideas — pairs share.
Let us discuss (p.176): fill in blanks — setting, tone, and capitalised letters.

time_bands.activity: Teacher returns briefly to the deity-stanza board list from the previous reading encounter, then frames the task: students will now identify the central idea each stanza carries.

Students work in pairs on the stanza-to-main-idea matching task from "Let us discuss" (p.176). Pairs note their stanza numbers on their books; teacher circulates and probes with questions like "What does the Men's stanza ask for — gratitude or request?"

Whole-class debrief of the matching task, then move to the fill-in-the-blank task on p.176. Teacher reads each blank aloud and takes two or three student responses before confirming — focusing especially on why 'h' is capitalised in Hands, Heart, Home.

Quick consolidation: teacher summarises the tone (celebratory and humble) and the setting (rural harvest festival) in two sentences. Students write one sentence in their books — their own statement of the poem's overall tone.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the hymn aloud and mapped the deity-stanza structure, students are now ready to articulate the main idea each stanza carries. A common difficulty is confusing the idea of stanza 2 (Varuna/rain as mercy) with stanza 4 (Brahma as universal creator) — contrast 'mercy that fostered our grain' with 'Seed and Scythe of our harvests' explicitly. The capitalised Hands, Heart, Home in stanza 4 signals divine inhabitation of human action — worth a pointed question to the class.

periods.activity_title: Literary Devices in the Hymn — Identification and Analysis

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.177): identify poetic device in two given lines.
Let us think and reflect (p.177): match lines to expressions and name the poetic device.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.177): find repetitions in the poem and state the poet's purpose — self-study.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly recaps the devices students already know — personification, alliteration, metaphor, imagery — by eliciting one example of each from any poem they recall. This frames the vocabulary students will need for today's tasks.

Students work individually on the device-identification task from "Let us think and reflect" (p.177) — two lines: 'Bright and munificent lord of the morn!' and 'We bring thee our lives and our labours for tribute.' Teacher invites two or three responses and discusses why the second line is alliteration.

Teacher models the three-column matching task (p.177) with the first row, then pairs complete the remaining rows — matching lines to expressions and naming the device from the box (imagery, alliteration, simile, metaphor, personification). Class debrief focuses on why 'Thou art the Seed and the Scythe' is metaphor, not simile.

Teacher flags the repetition task on p.177 as a self-study item students can explore at home, briefly noting that the poet uses repetition to build a litany-like rhythm. No in-class time is allocated to it today.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked through the poem's main ideas and tone, students now analyse how Naidu's language creates effect. The most common confusion at this stage is labelling 'sweet and omnipotent mother, O Earth' as metaphor rather than personification — the Earth is not compared to a mother but addressed as one. Keep the device definitions visible on the board throughout. The repetition task on p.177 is flagged to students as a worthwhile self-study item that enriches understanding of the hymn's musical quality.

periods.activity_title: Symbolism and Extract Analysis — Surya and Brahma Stanzas

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.177): match symbols — Prithvi, Surya, Varuna — to their meanings.
Let us think and reflect (p.178): extract 1 questions — songs/garlands, gold, mellowing radiance, cymbal and flute.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces symbolism as a concept — a word or image that carries a meaning beyond its literal sense — and elicits one quick example from the students. Then pairs complete the symbol-matching task on p.177, connecting Prithvi, Surya, and Varuna to their symbolic meanings.
Quick whole-class check of the symbol matches; teacher consolidates by explaining that Naidu chose these deities to embody the three physical forces farmers depend on — light, water, and soil.

Students read Extract 1 (p.178) silently, then work individually on its four questions — the MCQ on songs and garlands, the fill-in on 'gold', the short-answer on 'mellowing radiance', and the fill-in on cymbal and flute. Teacher circulates and prompts students who are stuck on the metaphorical meaning of 'gold'.
Brief whole-class share: teacher takes one response per question, confirms or redirects, and underlines that 'gold of our fields' is metaphorical — ripeness and abundance, not the metal.

periods.teacher_notes: Having identified literary devices, students now read the poem for deeper symbolic meaning. The pairing of symbolism with Extract 1 works well here because the Surya stanza is the most concrete of the four, grounding abstract symbolism in images students can picture — light, crops, musical instruments. A common error is reading 'gold of our fields' literally; the teacher's prompt about what the fields produce at harvest should redirect this quickly.

periods.activity_title: Extract Analysis — Brahma Stanza and Comprehension Questions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.178–179): extract 2 questions — being, Seed and Scythe, eternal presence, chorus.
Let us think and reflect (p.179): answer questions — rain, wealth of valleys, manifold gladness, labours for tribute.

time_bands.activity: Students read Extract 2 (p.178–179) aloud in pairs — alternating lines — then work individually on its four questions: the MCQ on 'being', the true/false on 'Seed and Scythe', the phrase-identification SCR, and the SCR on how the lines signal a chorus. Teacher circulates and pauses at the true/false to discuss the duality of creation and harvest.

Whole-class debrief of Extract 2: teacher unpacks 'Father eternal' as timeless presence and 'ineffable Om' as beyond description, confirming the phrase-identification answers. The chorus signal — 'All Voices' as the speaker tag — is established clearly.

Students answer the four factual short-answer questions on p.179 individually — why farmers hail the rain god, what 'wealth of our valleys' refers to, why Earth is a 'source of manifold gladness', and why labours are offered as tribute. Teacher takes responses orally in sequence and writes key phrases on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: Having explored the Surya stanza and the poem's symbolism, students now work with the culminating Brahma stanza — the most philosophically dense of the four. The metaphor of God as 'Seed and Scythe' encapsulates the Hindu concept of divine as both source and end of creation; students often read it as agricultural description only, missing the existential layer. The four short-answer questions on p.179 ground the discussion in specific textual evidence and should follow naturally from Extract 2.

periods.activity_title: Reflective and Extended Response — Naidu's Craft and Vision

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.179): ECR — why three distinct voices; how the poem creates rural atmosphere.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the two extended-response prompts on p.179 aloud: why Naidu used separate voices for men, women, and all; and how she creates the sensory atmosphere of a rural harvest. Students spend a few minutes noting two or three ideas for each prompt before discussion opens.

Small groups of four discuss both prompts, with one member noting key points. Teacher circulates and prompts groups that focus only on content to consider Naidu's structural and sonic choices — instruments, anaphora, the progression from elemental deities to the universal creator.

Two or three groups share their responses; teacher builds a class response on the board — why the multi-voice structure represents the whole farming community, and which images (cymbals, flutes, garlands, gold of fields) recreate the festival atmosphere.
Students write one closing sentence in their books: a personal response to how Naidu's structural choice of distinct voices adds meaning to the hymn.

periods.teacher_notes: Having answered the factual comprehension questions, students now engage with the poem's design: why three voices, and how sensory language evokes the harvest scene. The most common thin response is listing images without explaining their effect — prompt students to say what each image does to the reader, not just what it depicts. The 'why is it a hymn' question on p.179 is closely related and can be woven into the closing consolidation without becoming a separate task.

periods.activity_title: Farming Implements, Synonyms, and Archaic Words

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.180): match farming implement pictures to uses and complete their names.
Let us learn (p.180–181): choose correct synonyms for underlined words using context clues.
Let us learn (p.181): find modern equivalents for archaic words using a dictionary.

time_bands.activity: Students examine the farming implement pictures in the textbook (p.180) and complete the matching task — implement image to its use — then fill in the missing letters to complete each implement's name. Teacher circulates and helps students who are unfamiliar with the tools by describing how each is held or moved.

Students read the synonym task on pp.180–181: for each sentence, they circle the context clue and then choose the matching synonym from the box (generous, help, brightness, indescribable, kind). Teacher models the first example (beneficent → kind) and then students work individually on munificent, succour, radiance, and ineffable.

In pairs, students use dictionaries to find modern equivalents for the five archaic words on p.181 — morrow, hither, quoth, betwixt, yonder. Pairs share one word each; teacher confirms and writes modern equivalents on the board.

Brief consolidation: teacher connects the archaic vocabulary to the poem's formal, hymn-like register — Naidu uses 'thee', 'thy', 'thou', 'thine' for the same reason these archaic words carry solemnity.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit focuses entirely on vocabulary drawn from the poem and its thematic world. Students often guess synonyms from general knowledge rather than from the context clue in the sentence — insist they circle the clue phrase before choosing. The farming implements task is concrete and engaging but may slow down students who have no rural exposure; brief verbal descriptions of sickle, scythe, plough, trowel, rake, and spade will suffice to keep the pace.

periods.activity_title: Paddy Cultivation Talk — Listening for Sequence and Detail

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.181): number the seven paddy cultivation events in the correct order while listening.
Let us listen (p.181–182): listen again and choose the correct option for three questions.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the listening task: a spoken talk on paddy cultivation from farm to market. Students read the seven events listed on p.181 before listening begins — transplanting, ploughing, threshing, puddling, harvesting, irrigating, milling — so they know what to listen for.

Teacher reads the transcript aloud at a measured pace while students number the seven events in the order they hear them. No pauses mid-transcript; students hold their pencils and write their numbers as each step is mentioned.
Quick pair-check of the sequence; teacher confirms the correct order on the board: ploughing → puddling → irrigating → transplanting → harvesting → threshing → milling.

Teacher reads the transcript a second time; students answer the three multiple-choice questions on pp.181–182 — the main soil-preparation step, the time for seedlings to mature, and why grains are dried after threshing. Individual work, then whole-class share.

Brief discussion: teacher asks students which step in the process surprised them most and whether any of it connects to harvest festivals like those in the poem. One or two short verbal responses close the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit builds listening-for-sequence skills using a factual talk on paddy cultivation, which connects directly to the agrarian world of the hymn. The most common error in the sequencing task is confusing the order of puddling and sowing — the transcript states puddling precedes seed-sowing explicitly, so a second listen helps. Keep the board order visible after the pair-check so students can self-correct before the second listening.

periods.activity_title: Silent Letters and Harvest Festival Dish Presentation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.182): say aloud words with silent 'n' and silent 'b' — individual and choral practice.
Let us speak (p.182): group presentation on a harvest festival dish from your region using the given prompts.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the silent-letter patterns on p.182: 'n' is silent after 'm' at word-end (hymn, column, autumn, solemn); 'b' is silent before 'm' (womb, tomb, bomb, climb, comb). Teacher models each word, then the class repeats chorally. Individual students volunteer a word each.

Groups of four are formed and the presentation task from p.182 is explained: each group chooses a harvest festival dish from their region and prepares a short spoken presentation using the provided prompts — name, regional variants, ingredients, preparation, serving, taste, ritual, and personal memory. Groups spend this time planning aloud — no written scripts.

Three or four groups deliver their presentations (up to five minutes each); the class listens and one appreciative observation per group is invited after each presentation. Teacher notes spoken clarity and whether the prompts were all addressed.
Teacher closes with a brief observation on how the dish presentations mirror the poem's celebration of harvest — food, ritual, and community are threads linking both.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit moves between two distinct speaking modes — pronunciation practice and oral presentation. The silent-letter segment is brief but important: 'hymn' itself contains a silent 'n', so the poem's title becomes a living example. For the presentation, students from urban backgrounds may be uncertain about a harvest festival dish — encourage them to choose any seasonal food associated with a festival they know, broadening the brief as needed. Not all groups need to present if time does not allow; those who do not present orally have still planned and practised.

periods.activity_title: Farmer Gratitude Slogan and Millet Exploration Project

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.183): draft a creative slogan expressing gratitude to farmers for the school notice board.
Let us explore (p.184): discuss whether millets feature in your cuisine and plan a millet recipe booklet.

time_bands.activity: Teacher sets up the writing task from p.183: the school wants to express gratitude to farmers on the notice board. Three criteria are noted on the board — central idea, simple language, conciseness. Teacher reads two or three examples of effective slogans from other contexts so students have a register reference.

Students draft their slogans individually. Teacher circulates and offers feedback — is the central idea focused? Is the language simple? Is it genuinely brief? Students may revise once before writing a clean version. Two or three students share their slogan with the class; brief appreciative response is invited.

Teacher introduces the millet exploration task from p.184 — reading aloud the Pearl Millet information in the textbook. Groups of four are formed; each group discusses whether millets feature in their home cuisine and names one dish. One member notes the group's findings.

Groups briefly plan what a millet recipe booklet from their class might contain — categories of dishes, regions represented, how recipes might be laid out. A nominated member notes the group's plan. Teacher clarifies that finding actual recipes and compiling the booklet is an extension that can happen beyond class time.
Teacher draws both tasks together: the slogan and the millet project both express the poem's theme — recognising and honouring what the land and farmers provide.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit covers two spines that share the poem's central theme of gratitude and the land. For the slogan task, students often produce decorative but vague slogans — the focus criterion (gratitude to farmers specifically) and the brevity criterion (a slogan is not a paragraph) need emphasis. The millet project is introduced as a planning conversation rather than a complete artefact; the booklet compilation extends naturally beyond a single sitting and is honestly framed as such.

periods.activity_title: Chapter Synthesis — Voice, Gratitude, and Nature's Gifts

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with a provocation drawn from the poem itself: 'We bring thee our lives and our labours for tribute.' Ask students — what does it mean to offer your life and labour to something? Brief open-floor exchange; no single answer expected.

In groups of four, students revisit the poem's four-stanza structure and discuss two questions: how Naidu's choice to separate Men, Women, and All voices changes the meaning of the poem, and what the progression from elemental deities (Surya, Varuna, Prithvi) to the universal creator (Brahma) says about the farmers' worldview. Groups appoint a spokesperson.

Spokespersons share their group's key insight; teacher maps the responses on the board under two headings — 'Structure and Voice' and 'Nature and the Divine'. Teacher draws connections across the vocabulary (munificent, succour, radiance), the literary devices (anaphora, personification, metaphor), and the listening content on paddy cultivation, showing how each spine illuminated one facet of the same agricultural world.

Each student writes a final reflective paragraph — independently, beginning fresh — responding to: 'What does Harvest Hymn say about the relationship between human labour and the natural world?' Students draw on any content from the poem they found meaningful. Paragraphs are self-contained; no prior draft or homework is assumed.

One or two students read their paragraphs aloud. Teacher closes by noting that Naidu wrote this hymn to honour the voices least often heard in formal literature — the farming community — and that the poem's enduring power lies in making that gratitude collective and musical.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis draws together every aspect of the chapter — the poem's voice structure and deities, the literary devices, the vocabulary of harvest and devotion, the paddy cultivation process, and the theme of gratitude — without assuming any specific prior activity, discussion, or written piece. The reflective paragraph is designed to begin and close entirely within this sitting; students who have engaged with any part of the chapter will have something to say, regardless of which path they took through it. The synthesis is not a test — it is a space to connect.

items.item_stem: In Harvest Hymn, the Women's Voices address the Earth as "Sweet and omnipotent mother." Which of the following best describes the literary device used in this phrase?

options.label: A
options.text: Simile, because the Earth is compared to a mother using the word 'like'.

options.label: B
options.text: Personification, because the Earth is given the human quality of motherhood.

options.label: C
options.text: Alliteration, because several words beginning with the same sound appear together.

options.label: D
options.text: Imagery, because the phrase creates a picture of a woman standing in a field.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student confuses personification with simile, expecting a comparative word to signal figurative language.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student has identified an alliterative pattern elsewhere in the poem and is applying that label without checking the definition.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student treats any sensory phrase as imagery without distinguishing between the device that creates a picture and the one that assigns human qualities.

items.item_stem: In the final stanza of Harvest Hymn, the combined voices of men and women address Brahma with the lines beginning "Thou art the Seed and the Scythe of our harvests." Explain in two to three sentences what this metaphor reveals about the way the farming community understands Brahma's role, and why the poem places this address last rather than first.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The metaphor presents Brahma as both the origin of life (Seed) and the force that ends and gathers it (Scythe), showing the farming community believes the divine encompasses the entire cycle of creation and completion, not only one stage. Placing this address last moves the hymn from the physical and elemental — sun, rain, earth — to the universal and eternal, so the poem builds from the visible gifts of nature toward the invisible source behind them all.

items.item_stem:
After listening to the talk on paddy cultivation, arrange the following six steps in the order in which they occur according to the talk.

(1) Threshing
(2) Transplanting of seedlings
(3) Puddling
(4) Harvesting
(5) Milling
(6) Ploughing

options.label: A
options.text: Ploughing → Puddling → Transplanting → Harvesting → Threshing → Milling

options.label: B
options.text: Puddling → Ploughing → Transplanting → Threshing → Harvesting → Milling

options.label: C
options.text: Ploughing → Transplanting → Puddling → Harvesting → Milling → Threshing

options.label: D
options.text: Ploughing → Puddling → Harvesting → Transplanting → Threshing → Milling

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student has swapped puddling and ploughing, likely because puddling was emphasised as the 'most important' step and was remembered first.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student has placed transplanting before puddling, confusing the nursery-bed preparation sequence with the field-flooding sequence.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has confused harvesting and transplanting, perhaps because both involve physically moving plant material.

items.source_lo: Student sequences spoken procedural information and retrieves specific detail from an informational talk using a listening-to-respond mode.
items.source_context: Spoken talk on paddy cultivation: ploughing, puddling, transplanting, threshing, milling; rice as grass seed.
items.item_stem: The talk describes two separate reasons why certain steps in paddy cultivation require large amounts of water. In two sentences, identify each step that depends heavily on water and explain the specific role water plays at that stage, as stated in the talk.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Puddling requires the soil to be soaked with water to prepare it for planting — water softens and saturates the soil so it can hold moisture and support growth. After transplanting, the field must be kept continuously flooded through irrigation because paddy crops require waterlogged conditions to develop properly into mature rice plants.

items.item_stem: Choose a food or dish associated with a harvest festival or seasonal celebration you know. Describe it to the class: give its name, name its main ingredients, and explain one tradition or ritual connected with its preparation or serving.

expected_elements: Names the dish and links it clearly to a specific festival or season.
Mentions at least two main ingredients with brief description.
Describes one ritual, tradition, or memory connected to the dish.
Speaks in complete sentences with adequate volume and clarity.

items.item_stem: In Harvest Hymn, Sarojini Naidu celebrates the bond between farming communities and the land they cultivate. Speak for one to two minutes giving your opinion on this question: should harvest festivals be celebrated in urban schools and cities, or are they meaningful only in farming communities? Give at least two reasons to support your view.

expected_elements: States a clear opinion on celebrating harvest festivals beyond farming communities.
Gives at least two reasoned arguments supporting the stated view.
Connects at least one reason to the poem's theme of gratitude or interdependence.
Maintains a consistent position and concludes with a summary statement.

items.item_stem: Your school is celebrating World Food Day. Write a notice in no more than sixty words for the school notice board announcing the event and thanking the farming community for their contribution to the food on every plate. Include the event name, date, and one sentence of acknowledgement to farmers.

expected_elements: Notice includes event name, a plausible date, and school context.
Acknowledgement to farmers is specific and expressed in simple language.
Text stays within the word limit and reads as a notice, not a paragraph.
Tone is respectful and warm, matching the poem's spirit of gratitude.

items.item_stem: Imagine you are a young farmer who has just brought in the harvest after months of hard work. Write a short personal blog post of eighty to one hundred words describing how you feel at the end of harvest day and what you are grateful for. You may draw on the images of the field, the rain, the sun, or the community from Harvest Hymn to inspire your writing, but write entirely in your own voice.

expected_elements: Written in first person as a farmer; establishes an emotional tone.
Includes at least one specific image from the agrarian setting (sun, rain, field, crop).
Expresses a clear sense of gratitude or satisfaction rooted in personal experience.
Reads as a blog post — informal, reflective, and addressed to a general reader.

items.item_stem: Match each word from Harvest Hymn in Column A with its closest meaning in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
Column A|Column B
munificent|(i) help or support given in a time of need
succour|(ii) extremely generous; lavish in giving
radiance|(iii) beyond words; impossible to express
ineffable|(iv) bright, glowing light or warmth

answer_key.right: (i) help or support given in a time of need

items.item_stem:
The poem Harvest Hymn uses archaic English forms such as 'thee', 'thy', 'thou', and 'thine'. Read the two sentences below, which also use archaic words. Rewrite each sentence replacing the archaic word (given in parentheses) with its modern English equivalent, and in one sentence explain what effect the archaic language creates in a devotional poem like Harvest Hymn.

(a) Come (hither) and see the harvest laid out in the field.
(b) He stood (yonder), watching the rain fall on the ripened crop.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (a) Come here and see the harvest laid out in the field. (b) He stood over there, watching the rain fall on the ripened crop. Archaic language gives the poem a solemn, ceremonial tone that is fitting for a hymn addressed to divine figures, making the speakers' reverence feel formal and timeless.

items.item_stem: Harvest Hymn celebrates the gratitude of farming communities for the crops that sustain life. Millets — small-seeded grasses with high fibre and mineral content — have been grown and eaten across India for centuries. Write an extended response of one paragraph (eighty to one hundred words) explaining why millets can be considered a fitting symbol of the values expressed in the hymn, drawing on what you know about their nutritional importance and their place in traditional Indian farming and cuisine.

expected_elements: Connects millets to traditional Indian farming — longevity, regional diversity, or crop resilience.
References the nutritional value of millets — fibre, minerals — with at least one specific detail.
Links millet cultivation or consumption to the hymn's themes of gratitude, bounty, or interdependence.
Writes in coherent paragraph form with a clear central claim.

items.item_stem: Working in a group of three or four, design a two-page spread for a class millet recipe booklet. Your spread must include: (a) the name of one dish made with millets from your region or any region of India; (b) a list of its main ingredients; (c) a brief step-by-step preparation method in five to seven steps; and (d) a short note — three to four sentences — connecting this dish to the themes of harvest, gratitude, or community that Harvest Hymn celebrates. Present your completed spread to the class.

expected_elements: Dish is named and correctly identified as millet-based with regional grounding.
Ingredient list is plausible and specific; preparation steps are sequenced logically.
Connecting note links the dish to at least one theme from the poem — gratitude, harvest, or community.
Spread is presented clearly to the class with all four required elements visible.
